answer: Graph factorization (matrix factorization of the adjacency or proximity matrix, e.g., factorizing the node-by-node matrix so each node gets an embedding whose inner products approximate edge weights/links) is applicable to graphs where the adjacency or proximity relationships can be meaningfully captured in a matrix, typically undirected (and sometimes weighted) graphs of moderate size, since it requires forming and factorizing an n-by-n matrix (costly in time and memory for large graphs, and it is inherently a transductive, structure-only method that cannot naturally embed unseen nodes). It is generally applicable to homogeneous, single-relation networks, and it preserves first-order (direct link) proximity well but captures higher-order structure only if the matrix is explicitly constructed with it (e.g., via powers of the adjacency matrix), which becomes expensive. LINE (Large-scale Information Network Embedding) is applicable to large-scale, possibly weighted and directed or undirected information networks, including very large graphs with millions of nodes and edges, because it optimizes an edge-sampling objective with negative sampling (using stochastic gradient descent on edges rather than full matrix operations), scales linearly with the number of edges, and explicitly preserves both first-order proximity (directly connected nodes) and second-order proximity (nodes sharing neighbors). Thus, compared with graph factorization, LINE is applicable to a broader range of graph sizes and types (including directed and weighted graphs at scale) and handles higher-order proximity more efficiently, whereas graph factorization is limited to smaller, undirected-style matrix settings and is more computationally demanding, though both are structure-only, unsupervised, node-embedding approaches.
